clinicalPearls: The most common congenital viral infection and a leading non-genetic cause of sensorineural hearing loss and neurodevelopmental disability in children.
Most infected newborns are asymptomatic at birth, yet a proportion of these still go on to develop late-onset hearing loss.
Symptomatic disease may include small size for gestational age, microcephaly, petechiae, jaundice, hepatosplenomegaly, and low platelets.
Neurological features can include intracranial calcifications (often periventricular), chorioretinitis, and seizures.
Both primary maternal infection and non-primary (reactivation or reinfection) during pregnancy can transmit to the fetus, with primary infection carrying higher risk.
Diagnosis must be confirmed within the first three weeks of life to distinguish congenital from perinatally acquired infection, using viral detection from urine or saliva.
Because of the risk of progressive hearing loss, confirmed cases need structured audiological surveillance over time, not just a single newborn screen.
Antiviral therapy is considered for symptomatic infants, particularly those with central nervous system involvement, to improve hearing and neurodevelopmental outcomes.
reference.pathophysiology: Cytomegalovirus, a herpesvirus, crosses the placenta following maternal infection and disseminates in the fetus, where it replicates in multiple organs. The developing central nervous system is particularly vulnerable: infection disrupts neuronal migration and brain development and causes an inflammatory response that produces calcifications, microcephaly, and migrational abnormalities. Involvement of the inner ear leads to progressive sensorineural hearing loss, while infection of the liver, bone marrow, and reticuloendothelial system accounts for hepatosplenomegaly, thrombocytopenia, and jaundice.
additionalDifferentials: Other congenital infections in the TORCH group (toxoplasmosis, rubella, syphilis, herpes simplex, Zika)
Inherited metabolic or genetic disorders causing microcephaly
additionalInvestigations: CMV detection by PCR from urine or saliva within the first three weeks of life
Cranial imaging (ultrasound and/or MRI) for calcification and brain abnormalities
Full blood count, platelets, and liver function tests
Dried blood spot testing when late confirmation is needed
redFlags: Microcephaly or abnormal neuroimaging indicating central nervous system involvement
Confirmed or progressive sensorineural hearing loss
Symptomatic disease with thrombocytopenia, hepatitis, or petechiae
Failure to confirm the diagnosis within three weeks, losing the ability to prove congenital infection
reference.prognosis: Asymptomatic infants generally do well but remain at risk of late-onset hearing loss, warranting ongoing audiological follow-up; symptomatic infants, especially those with neurological involvement, have a higher risk of hearing loss, developmental delay, and other long-term deficits, though early antiviral therapy can improve outcomes in selected cases.
pitfalls: Missing the diagnostic window by testing after three weeks of age and being unable to distinguish congenital from acquired infection
Assuming a normal newborn hearing screen excludes future hearing loss
Overlooking asymptomatic infection, which still carries a risk of late sequelae
Attributing intracranial calcification solely to toxoplasmosis without confirming CMV
Failing to arrange long-term audiological and developmental surveillance
management: Treat symptomatic congenital infection, particularly with central nervous system involvement, with antiviral therapy using oral valganciclovir or intravenous ganciclovir to improve hearing and neurodevelopmental outcomes
Monitor during antiviral treatment for neutropenia and hepatotoxicity
Undertake serial audiological assessment with early hearing intervention such as hearing aids or cochlear implantation
Provide ophthalmological surveillance and treat chorioretinitis
Arrange neurodevelopmental follow-up with early intervention and therapy services
Withhold routine antivirals in asymptomatic infants but continue audiological surveillance for late-onset sensorineural hearing loss
Coordinate multidisciplinary follow-up across audiology, ophthalmology, neurology and paediatrics
